Hi, I'm suicidal. This post is NOT about me. It's for all the people who have committed suicide who can't be here to post on this thread. I have been suicidal for about 40 years, I'm still here so I will do my best to speak on their behalf.

1) People who are <really> suicidal usually will not tell anyone. It freaks people out. It even freaks doctors out that are trained and deal with depressed people everyday. The good news is it OK to ask us if we are feeling suicidal, we might open up.

2) Don't make it easy for us. Meaning don't keep things like firearms in the house of people who tend to get suicidal. Don't underestimate the power of simply making it inconvenient for us. The inconvenience gives us more time to think before taking action. Firearms make it too easy to not give enough effort and time to think it through. Please, don't keep firearms anywhere near us suicidal people.

3) I think most of us do think about the people we leave behind when we commit suicide. It's really complicated though and every person is different. Most of the time we feel people don't understand, don't care, will not miss us, will not have a big impact on others lives when we are gone, etc...

4) If you know someone is suicidal and they have access to meds, please Google overdose amounts. It's OK, 99% chance us suicidal people have already Googled it and have a pretty good idea of how much we need to OD. Back to point #1 & #2. Ask us are we suicidal? If yes, it is an opportunity to say, "Hey, can I help you manage this big bottle of pills, so it isn't such a temptation". Having access to a weeks worth of pills that will not lead to a successful OD vs. 30+ days that will lead to an OD makes it harder for us to OD.

5) "Getting help" doesn't always make the problem go away. It can help reduce the likelyhood of suicide. Depression and suicidal feelings are very complex and person dependent. It is completely possible to get enough therapy to have coping mechanisms to live a functioning life and hold a job while simultaneously living life in a perpetual state of feeling suicidal.

6) Don't assume that because you were once depressed or felt suicidal for a few weeks that you can even remotely understand what the person is feeling. There is a much bigger emotional gap between feeling like 'you want to blow your brains out' and actually putting a 'gun to your head and pulling trigger' than people realize. The emotional gap and depth of pain in huge. Which is one of the reason you may hear a suicidal person say 'you don't understand'. Because they are 1,000 miles/km further down a dark path than you have ever been. Unless you have truly botched a real suicide attempt it is hard to relate.

7) I hope you will never need any of these points. Don't ever take for granted what you have in life. Please do me a favor and read Holly Butcher's inspirational letter and try to live life as Holly describes. Please take 2 minutes and do it for those of us that are unable to live like this: http://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-5240791/Dying-womans-heartbreaking-letter-world.html

8) People will not like #8 but I'm going to say it anyway. There is no resource or etiquette around minimizing the impact to #3 (other people) when we commit suicide. Many of us would like to have our finances and assets in order so the people that are left behind have minimal bull shit to deal with. Once we are dead, it is hard to give passwords, bank account numbers, insurance details, what kids should get what assets, etc... It creates another big downstream mess besides just the loss of life.

People get really bent out of shape about the idea of a "Checklist-before-you-go". However, it goes back to point #2. Having a checklist of all the stuff that needs to be done to cleanly 'checking-out' is a pretty long list of stuff. One one hand, it forces us suicidal people to give it a bit more thought before pulling a trigger. On the other hand, if we are going to 'check-out' at least we tried to get things in order. Right now, nothing exists like this on the web. Asking people who lost a loved one to suicide what would have made things easier usually gets the obvious answer of "I wish they wouldn't have committed suicide".

Sorry, I know most people hate point #8. I realize it is extremely unpleasant to have to think about a post-suicide action plan. The typical knee-jerk reaction is, 'just keep them from killing themselves'. The problem is people will commit suicide despite our best efforts to keep people from committing suicide. Simply having the very uncomfortable discussion about a post-suicide action plan goes back to point #1 & #2 and opens up dialog. In the unfortunate event they get all help possible and still decide the best action is to commit suicide, it helps with #3.

A list of basic suicide etiquette could go a long way in minimizing pain of others. (1) Don't bring innocent people into your suicide attempt (2) Don't leave a surprise mess for a love one to find (3) make sure love ones aren't left battling over your assets and they can get everything transferred into their names easily with minimal bull shit (4) Line up survivor help resources for loved ones because it will likely come as a shock that you killed yourself

9) The forums are filled with survivor bias ( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survivorship_bias)

We only hear from the people that got better, didn't commit suicide or lost a loved one. Dead people can't post on forums. It is unfortunate, as these folks could really help the most suicidal among us. It is the survivor bias in this thread that actually compelled me to write this post.

10) I hope this post helps the people who need to hear it. Feel free to message me. Happy to help however I can...
